# **World Clock and Interregional Synchronisms Across the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East, c. 1800–1500 BCE (Lane W2)**

To anchor a real-time 3D reconstruction of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East at **c. 1650 BCE** (within the broader **1800–1500 BCE** window), every regional sequence must be locked to a single master calendar1. Across this 300-year horizon, dendrochronologically sequenced radiocarbon wiggle-matching supports the **Mesopotamian Middle Chronology** (or Low-Middle Chronology, 8 years lower)2, while Bayesian radiocarbon modeling on short-lived plant material places the **Late Minoan IA (LM IA) Thera eruption** in the late 17th or early 16th century BCE (**\~1606–1589 BCE** at 68.3% probability on IntCal20), prior to the reign of Pharaoh Ahmose and the start of the Egyptian New Kingdom3.  
At **c. 1650 BCE**, the interconnected world is situated in the **Middle Bronze Age IIB–IIC / Second Intermediate Period** horizon: Crete is transitioning from **Middle Minoan III (MM III)** into **early LM IA** (under the Aegean High Chronology) with flourishing Neopalatial palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia1; mainland Greece is in the **Shaft Grave Period (MH III–LH I)** at Mycenae (Grave Circle B)1; Egypt is divided between the waning **13th Dynasty** / **14th Dynasty** and the rising **15th ("Hyksos") Dynasty** at Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a, expanding to \~250 hectares) alongside the **16th and 17th Dynasties** at Thebes3; **Hattusili I** is establishing the **Old Hittite Kingdom** at Hattusa (1650–1620 BCE, Middle Chronology)10; **Ammi-ditana** and **Ammi-saduqa** rule late Old Babylonian Mesopotamia alongside the secessionist **First Sealand Dynasty** in the south13; and **Classic Kerma** (*Kerma Classique*) rules Upper and Lower Nubia16.

## **Section 1: Summary**

* **World clock synchronization at c. 1650 BCE:** Setting the project clock to 1650 BCE pairs the **Mesopotamian Middle Chronology** (supported by Anatolian juniper dendro-¹⁴C wiggle-matching) with the **Egyptian Second Intermediate Period chronology** and the **Aegean High/IntCal20 Chronology**, which places 1650 BCE near the **MM III / LM IA** and **MH III / LH I** transitions rather than in the Protopalatial period (Claims 1–12)1.  
* **Thera eruption predates the Egyptian 18th Dynasty:** Direct IntCal20 radiocarbon dating of museum objects from the 17th to early 18th Dynasties—including C4 straw from a mudbrick of Pharaoh Ahmose's temple at Abydos (1542–1427 cal BCE, 66.4% probability)—indicates that the LM IA Thera eruption (\~1606–1589 BCE at 68.3% probability; \~1609–1560 BCE at 95.4% probability) occurred during the Second Intermediate Period and predates Ahmose (Claims 1–4)3.  
* **Egypt at c. 1650 BCE (Avaris and the Hyksos transition):** Around 1650–1640 BCE, the eastern Nile Delta port of **Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a)** transitioned from the **14th Dynasty** (c. 1710–1640 BCE, including King Nehesi) to the **15th ("Hyksos") Dynasty** (c. 1640–1530 BCE in Bietak's chronology; 1650–1550 BCE in Shaw's conventional chronology), while the late **13th Dynasty** (1759–1630 BCE in Hornung et al. 2006\) gave way to the **16th and 17th Dynasties** at Thebes (Claims 14–21, 57–58)8.  
* **Tell el-Dab'a Minoan-style frescoes postdate 1650 BCE:** The Minoan-style *buon fresco* wall paintings of bull-leapers, labyrinth patterns, and Knossian griffins from Palaces F and G at **'Ezbet Helmi (Tell el-Dab'a Phase C/3)** date to the **early 18th Dynasty** (Hatshepsut and the first half of Thutmose III, c. 1500–1450 BC / c. 1479–1457 BC), not the Hyksos period, and must be excluded from a c. 1650 BCE reconstruction of Avaris (Claims 41–42)22.  
* **Earlier Levantine palaces featured Aegean-style murals in the Middle Bronze Age:** Unlike Tell el-Dab'a, Aegean-style frescoes adorned the Middle Bronze Age palaces of **Alalakh Level VII** (destroyed by Hattusili I before c. 1628 BC Middle Chronology, with earlier wall plaster fragments and a MM IIB–IIIA Kamares sherd sealed beneath the Level VII floor) and **Tel Kabri Phase III** (modeled by IntCal13 radiocarbon to end \~1700 BC, though dated ceramic-typologically by Bietak to shortly before 1500 BC), while **Qatna's Room N** paintings belong to the Late Bronze Age (15th–14th century BC) (Claims 24–26a, 29–30, 43–46)23.  
* **Anatolia and the founding of the Old Hittite Kingdom at c. 1650 BCE:** Following the destruction of **Kanesh (Kültepe) Level Ib** (c. 1710–1700 BC), which ended the Old Assyrian colony network after the reigns of **Pithana** and **Anitta** of Kussara, **Hattusili I** (1650–1620 BCE, Middle Chronology) rebuilt **Hattusa** as his capital around ca. 1650 BCE, campaigned into northern Syria, and was succeeded by his grandson **Mursili I** (1620–1590 BCE), who sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE (Claims 33–36)10.  
* **Mesopotamia split between Old Babylon and the Sealand Dynasty:** Under the Middle Chronology, **Hammurabi** reigned 1792–1750 BCE, and around 1650 BCE Babylon was ruled by **Ammi-ditana** (1684–1647 BC) and **Ammi-saduqa** (1646–1626 BCE), while southernmost Mesopotamia (including **Tell Khaiber**) was controlled by the secessionist **First Sealand Dynasty** (c. 1720–1475 BCE, founded by **Ili-ma-ilu**) until Mursili I sacked Babylon under **Samsu-ditana** (1625–1595 BCE) in 1595 BCE (Claims 8, 37–39)2.  
* **The Khyan lid at Knossos and Edfu sealings:** An alabaster lid bearing the cartouche of 15th Dynasty Hyksos king **Seuserenre Khyan** found in the North Lustral Basin at **Knossos** in a **MM IIIA** pottery deposit links Hyksos Egypt to Neopalatial Crete, while clay sealings of Khyan found alongside 13th Dynasty king **Sobekhotep IV** at **Tell Edfu** and in early SIP levels at **Tell el-Dab'a** support placing Khyan earlier in the 17th century BCE than previously assumed (Claims 39a–40, 47–48)31.  
* **Three-way synchronism linking Egypt, Byblos, and Mari/Babylon:** A relief at **Byblos** showing 13th Dynasty Pharaoh **Neferhotep I** (c. 1721–1710 BCE in Hornung et al. 2006\) opposite Prince **Yantin-('Ammu)** of Byblos—who is also recorded in the **Mari archives** of **Zimri-Lim** (c. 1780–1760 B.C., contemporary with **Hammurabi** of Babylon)—links the mid-13th Dynasty to the Middle Chronology of Syria and Mesopotamia (Claims 22–23, 49–50a)9.  
* **Mari tablets document Cretan (*Kaptara*) trade at Ugarit:** Cuneiform tablet **A 1270** and related texts from **Mari** record tin shipped from the direction of Iran via Mari to **Aleppo**, **Hazor** (under King **Ibni-Addu**), and **Ugarit**, where tin was issued to a man from **Kaptara (Crete)** and an interpreter resident at Ugarit, alongside Kaptarite inlaid weapons and silver vessels exchanged between royal courts (Claims 28–28a, 50–51)37.  
* **Byblos and Avaris urban profiles at c. 1650 BCE:** **Avaris** grew into an expansive **250-hectare** Delta harbour metropolis centered on a **450 × 400 m** interior harbour basin, Canaanite broad-room temples (worshipping the Syrian Storm God/Seth), and a royal palace district at 'Ezbet Helmi, whereas **Byblos** was a compact (**\~5-hectare**) fortified coastal acropolis built around a sacred spring, featuring the **Temple of the Obelisks**, the *Temple à Escalier*, and a cedarwood and *kpny*\-shipbuilding monopoly whose direct ties to Avaris weakened during the 15th Dynasty (Claims 19, 22–23, 55–58)3.  
* **Nubia (Classic Kerma) and the Hyksos–Kushite axis:** During **Classic Kerma** (ca. 1750–1550 BC / 1750–1500 BC), the **25-hectare** capital at **Kerma** (centered on the **Western Deffufa** temple, palace, and royal tumuli) projected power north into Lower Nubia (Buhen) and maintained diplomatic and trade ties across the desert oasis route with the Hyksos at Avaris, culminating in **Apophis's** intercepted alliance letter to the **Ruler of Kush** recorded on the **Second Stela of Kamose** (Claims 40a, 54\)16.

## **Topic C: Byblos and Avaris at c. 1650 BCE**

### **Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a, Eastern Nile Delta)**

Around 1650–1640 BCE, Avaris (*Hutwaret*) expanded across sand turtlebacks east of the Pelusiac branch of the Nile (30–40 km south of the Mediterranean coast) to cover approximately **250 hectares (2.5 sq km)**, making it the largest city in the Eastern Mediterranean3. At the center of the city lay an interior **harbour basin measuring approximately 450 × 400 m**, fed by seasonal sea-water inflow and Nile channels that provided year-round maritime navigation8. The urban fabric combined Egyptian and Near Eastern residential and funerary quarters ('Ezbet Rushdi, 'Ezbet Helmi, Area A, Area F)8. Its sacred precincts housed Canaanite broad-room sanctuaries (such as **Temple III** and **Temple F2**) and a **Temple Precinct of the Syrian Storm God** (venerated as a protector of sailors and syncretized with Egyptian Seth)8. On the western riverbank at **'Ezbet Helmi (Area H)**, the Hyksos royal district included a **Palace of King Khayan**8 and, in the late Hyksos period (Phase D/2), a **6.20 m (12-cubit) buttressed mudbrick fortification wall**, enclosed gardens, and a monumental **31.5 × 27.1 m casemate building**25. Politically, around 1650–1640 BCE, Avaris transitioned from the local Levantine **14th Dynasty** (c. 1710–1640 BCE, including **King Nehesi**, whose dynasty possibly descended from the royal line of Byblos) to the **15th ("Hyksos") Dynasty** (c. 1640–1530 BCE in Bietak's chronology; 1650–1550 BCE in Shaw's), whose attested rulers include **Sakir-Har**, **Khyan (Seuserenra)**, **Apophis**, and **Khamudi**8. Avaris operated as a major maritime and overland hub importing Levantine Canaanite jars, Cypriot White Painted wares, and Near Eastern sphendonoid hematite balance weights, while exporting Tell el-Yahudiyeh juglets and Egyptian Marl C vessels to Ashkelon, Cyprus, Kerma, and Thera3.

### **Byblos (Gubla, Modern Jbeil, Lebanese Coast)**

Bronze Age Byblos occupied a coastal promontory of **approximately 5 hectares**, though the extent of its Middle Bronze Age lower town remains unknown beneath modern Jbeil8. Its fortified acropolis had an organic, circular layout centered on a **deep-water spring** (accessed via a spiraling staircase), with closely packed houses lacking courtyards and a more rectangular street grid south of the central temples8. At least four major temple precincts ringed the central spring8, including the **Temple of the Obelisks** (built over the burnt Early Bronze Age L-shaped Temple and containing over 40 standing stones and obelisks, among them the hieroglyphic **Abishemu Obelisk**, DGA 17917\)42, the **Temple Oriental**, the **Temple of Ba'alat Gebal** (Lady of Byblos), and the **Temple à Escalier** (a broad-room temple *in antis* on a square platform facing the harbour with five stone anchor ex-votos embedded in its staircase)8, alongside the rock-cut shaft **Royal Tombs (Tombs I–IV)** on the seaward cliff49. Earlier MB II rulers of Byblos—including **Abi-shemu** (Tomb I), **Ip-shemu-abi / Abishemou-Abi** (Tomb II), and **Yantin-('Ammu)** (contemporary with 13th Dynasty Pharaoh Neferhotep I and Zimri-Lim of Mari)—used the Egyptian title *ḥꜣty-ʻ n Kpny* ("Mayor/Governor of Byblos") and wrote in Egyptian hieroglyphs38. Economically, Byblos held a virtual monopoly on high-grade **Lebanon cedar timber**, cedar pitch for mummification, and the construction of seagoing ***kpny*****\-ships** for the Egyptian crown; however, Bietak (2023) notes that after the 14th Dynasty (c. 1710–1640 BCE), direct trade ties between Byblos and Avaris were largely interrupted during the 15th Dynasty Hyksos period (c. 1640–1530 BCE)8.

## **Assumptions checked**

* **W2-1:** **Confirmed** (with a \~10-year chronological boundary nuance: under Shaw 2000 and High/Radiocarbon chronologies the 15th "Hyksos" Dynasty begins ca. 1650 BCE, whereas under Bietak 2023 and Hornung et al. 2006 the transition at Avaris from the 14th/13th Dynasties to the 15th Dynasty occurs at c. 1640/1630 BCE) (Claims 14, 15, 18, 19, 57\)3.  
* **W2-2:** **Confirmed** (in the Mesopotamian Middle Chronology—supported by Anatolian dendro-radiocarbon wiggle-matching—Hammurabi reigned 1792–1750 BCE and Babylon fell to the Hittite king Mursili I in 1595 BCE) (Claims 8, 36, 37, 38\)2.  
* **W2-3:** **Partly confirmed** (Byblos was a Middle Bronze Age city-state with deep, centuries-long cedar, shipbuilding, and dynastic ties to Egypt during the 12th–14th Dynasties up to c. 1640 BCE, though Bietak 2023 notes that direct ties between Byblos and Avaris were largely interrupted during the 15th Dynasty Hyksos period, c. 1640–1530 BCE) (Claims 19, 22, 22a, 23, 49, 55, 56\)8.  
* **W2-4:** **Confirmed** (the Minoan-style *buon fresco* wall paintings from Palaces F and G at 'Ezbet Helmi / Tell el-Dab'a date to Phase C/3 in the early 18th Dynasty—specifically Hatshepsut and the first half of Thutmose III, c. 1500–1450 BC / c. 1479–1457 BC—and not the Hyksos period) (Claims 41, 42\)22.  
* **W2-5:** **Partly confirmed** (the alabaster lid inscribed with the cartouche of 15th Dynasty Hyksos king Seuserenre Khyan was excavated by Evans in the North Lustral Basin at Knossos in a deposit of **Middle Minoan IIIA** pottery, tying Khyan to MM III Crete, though specialists debate whether its deposition reflects a contemporary gift or a later heirloom/*terminus post quem*) (Claims 47, 48\)31.  
* **W2-6:** **Confirmed** (under the Middle Chronology, Hattusili I founded the Old Hittite Kingdom and rebuilt Hattusa as its capital in the mid-17th century BCE, reigning 1650–1620 BCE) (Claims 35, 36\)10.

## **Debates**

### **1\. Date of the Thera Eruption and Aegean High vs. Low Chronology**

Proponents of the **Aegean High / Modified High Chronology** (Sturt W. Manning, Hendrik J. Bruins, Johannes van der Plicht, and Felix Höflmayer) rely on Bayesian modeling of short-lived plant radiocarbon datasets from Thera, Crete, and the Aegean calibrated with **IntCal20**3. While IntCal20's tree-ring revision across the 1620–1540 BCE plateau shifted the eruption date slightly downward from earlier \~1628 BCE proposals, Manning (2022, 2024\) calculates a 68.3% probability range of **\~1606–1589 BCE** (or 1612–1602 BCE, peak \~1608 BCE; 95.4% range \~1609–1560 BCE), and Bruins & van der Plicht (2025) show via direct ¹⁴C dating of Pharaoh Ahmose's mudbrick straw (1542–1427 cal BCE, 66.4% probability) that the Thera eruption predates Ahmose and falls in the Second Intermediate Period3. Conversely, proponents of the **Aegean Low / Short Chronology** (Peter Warren, Vronwy Hankey, Manfred Bietak, and Malcolm H. Wiener) date the LM IA Thera eruption to **1530–1525 BC** (or 1550–1500 BC during the early 18th Dynasty)45. They cite Egyptian "baggy" calcite vases in Mycenae Shaft Graves IV and V (argued to be 18th Dynasty forms), identical gold ring impressions in LM IA Thera and final LM IB Crete (which would span 5–6 generations under the High Chronology vs. 3 generations under the Low Chronology), and Thera pumice appearing at Tell el-Dab'a in 18th Dynasty Phase C/3–2 workshops31.

### **2\. Chronology of the Levant Middle Bronze Age II/III Transition and the Tel Kabri Wall Paintings**

In the southern Levant, Felix Höflmayer, Assaf Yasur-Landau, and Eric H. Cline (2016, 2017\) support a **High Levant MBA Chronology** based on Bayesian modeling (**IntCal13**) of short-lived radiocarbon samples from Phases IV and III of the Canaanite palace at **Tel Kabri**27. Their Model A places the destruction of the Phase III palace—and its Aegean-style miniature wall and floor frescoes—at **\~1700 BC**, aligning with high ¹⁴C dates from Tell el-Dab'a, Tel Ifshar, and Tell el-Burak and implying that Kabri's frescoes predate the LM IA frescoes at Akrotiri by nearly a century27. In contrast, Manfred Bietak (2007, 2013\) defends a **Low Levant MBA Chronology** anchored to Tell el-Dab'a's historical datum lines, placing the MB II/III transition at **\~1590 BC**23. Pointing to Black Lustrous Wheelmade and Chocolate-on-White pottery in Tomb 902 at Tel Kabri, Bietak argues that the Tel Kabri palace and its frescoes remained in use until **shortly before 1500 BC** (terminal MB IIC / early 18th Dynasty)23.

### **3\. Chronological Placement of Hyksos King Khyan and Overlap of the 13th and 15th Dynasties**

Nadine Moeller, Gregory Marouard, Irene Forstner-Müller, and Felix Höflmayer argue for an **early placement of Khyan**, noting that 40 clay sealings of 15th Dynasty Hyksos king **Khyan** were found alongside sealings of 13th Dynasty king **Sobekhotep IV** in a single abandonment horizon at **Tell Edfu**, and that early Khyan sealings occur in Stratum E/1 (Area R/III) at **Tell el-Dab'a**, indicating Khyan ruled early in the 15th Dynasty (17th century BCE) and overlapped with the mid/late 13th Dynasty32. This earlier placement also aligns with the Khyan alabaster lid found in a **MM IIIA** context at Knossos under the Aegean High Chronology31. Conversely, Kim Ryholt (1997), Manfred Bietak, and Alexander Ilin-Tomich maintain a **traditional separation** of up to a century between Sobekhotep IV and Khyan, arguing that the Edfu ceramic assemblage postdates Sobekhotep IV and that the 13th Dynasty sealings at Edfu represent reused royal seals or residual debris rather than contemporary co-rule34.

### **4\. Mesopotamian and Hittite Absolute Chronology (Middle vs. Low Chronology)**

Sturt W. Manning, Gojko Barjamovic, and colleagues (2016) wiggle-matched high-precision ¹⁴C measurements on long Juniperus tree-ring sequences from Kültepe, Acemhöyük, and Karahöyük tied to the Old Assyrian Revised Eponym List (REL) and Shamshi-Adad I's death in Year 18 of Hammurabi2. Their results indicate that only the **Middle Chronology** (Hammurabi 1792–1750 BCE; Hattusili I 1650–1620 BCE; Mursili I's sack of Babylon 1595 BCE) or the **Low-Middle Chronology** (8 years lower, Fall of Babylon 1587 BCE) fits the physical wood and historical links2. Proponents of the **Low / Short and Ultra-Low Chronologies** rely on alternative astronomical solutions to the Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa and compressed ceramic stratigraphy (e.g., Gasche et al. 1998\) to lower dates by 64 years (Hammurabi 1728–1686 BCE, Fall of Babylon 1531 BCE) or 88–96 years (Fall of Babylon 1507 or 1499 BCE), though Manning et al. (2016) showed these lower schemes would place Kültepe Old Palace eponyms 20 to 90 years *after* the subsequent Waršama Palace was already constructed2.

## **Could not verify**

* **Named rulers of Crete, the Cyclades, Mainland Greece, and Cyprus (c. 1700–1550 BCE):** Because Linear A and Cypro-Minoan remain undeciphered and Mainland Greece was pre-literate during MH III–LH I, no personal names of Minoan, Cycladic, Early Mycenaean, or Middle/Late Cypriot rulers could be verified from contemporary primary texts64.  
* **Named ruler of Byblos at the exact year c. 1650 BCE:** While the 18th-century BCE rulers of Byblos (**Abi-shemu**, **Ip-shemu-abi**, and **Yantin-'Ammu**) are attested in the Byblos Royal Tombs, the Obelisk Temple, and the Mari archives, and Bietak (2023) notes that the 14th Dynasty at Avaris (c. 1710–1640 BCE) possibly descended from the royal line of Byblos, the specific personal name of the king reigning on the Byblos acropolis at 1650 BCE could not be verified from the available primary sources8.  
* **Total urban area of the lower town of Byblos in the Middle Bronze Age:** While Pfälzner (2012) gives an overall size of approximately **5 hectares** for the coastal kingdom mound of Byblos, Bietak (2023) states that an exact area measurement for the Middle Bronze Age lower town cannot be verified because it lies unexplored beneath modern settlements8.  
* **Named rulers of Classic Kerma (Kush) at c. 1650 BCE:** While Egyptian texts and sealings attest to the title *"Son of Re, Ruler of Kush"* (*sA \[Ra\] HqA n(.y) KSi*) and Execration Texts name earlier Kushite princes (such as *\&r(i)Ahi*), Cooper (2018) demonstrated that the supposed late SIP king *"Nedjeh"* on the Buhen Stele of Ka is an epithet (*"victorious ruler"*), leaving the personal names of the mid-17th to mid-16th century BCE kings of Classic Kerma unverified17.
